report:
## Report

The evidence does not fully support "yes" — regular vitamin C does **not** prevent colds for most people, though it has modest benefits.

The most authoritative source, the Cochrane systematic review of placebo-controlled trials (≥0.2 g/day), found that regular vitamin C supplementation had **no effect on cold incidence in the general population** (pooled RR 0.97, 29 comparisons, >11,000 participants), leading the authors to conclude "routine vitamin C supplementation is not justified" (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782, cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4/full).

However, there are two notable exceptions/nuances:
1. **Extreme physical stress**: In five trials of marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers in subarctic conditions, regular vitamin C supplementation cut cold *incidence* roughly in half (RR ~0.48–0.52) — a much stronger effect than in the general population (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/; nutraingredients.com/Article/2013/02/15/...).
2. **Duration and severity**: Even in the general population, regular (not therapeutic/after-onset) supplementation consistently shortened cold duration by about 8–10% and reduced severity by around 15% in a more recent meta-analysis (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544; link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8).

Taking vitamin C only after symptoms start showed no benefit.

**Conclusion**: For the average person, regular vitamin C intake does not prevent catching a cold, but it may modestly shorten and lessen the severity of colds when experienced, and it does meaningfully reduce risk for people under heavy physical/cold stress (athletes, soldiers). So the "yes" answer is only partially correct and should be qualified.
